No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest

A prosecutor in New York now says he did not have access to full transcripts of a woman's
account of being raped at Cornell University in 2024 when he decided not to pursue the
case.
District Attorney Matthew Van Houten says he stopped the investigation after only reviewing
the woman's signed statement.
NPR's Brian Mann reports.
Van Houten has said the former student who alleged in a recent civil lawsuit that she
was gang-raped by seven male students gave a different account to campus police two years
ago describing her participation in drug use and sex at a frat party as "voluntary, conscious,
and consensual."
But now more full transcripts of the woman's interviews with campus police investigators
have been reported by multiple news outlets.
They show she described the incident at the time in graphic terms as rape.
In a statement to WSKG Radio, Van Houten says he didn't see that information before stopping
the investigation.
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to
police Van Houten said," Brian Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
Starting today, states will be paying for a larger share of the bill to run the food
assistance program known as SNAP.
NPR's Julianna Kim reports.
Last year's massive Republican tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
included major changes to how SNAP is funded, shifting more of the costs onto states rather
than the federal government.
As a result, states may need to spend two to three times more in the future in order
to keep the food assistance program running.
That's according to the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality.
The key question now is how states will afford these new costs to SNAP.
Policy experts say states may need to raise taxes, cut funding for other programs, or
reduce access to food benefits.
When it comes as SNAP participation is already rapidly dropping.
Julianna Kim, NPR News.
A group of mathematicians is calling for better vetting of new results from artificial intelligence.
As NPR's Jeff Bronfield explains, this comes after one AI company claimed a major discovery.
The independent group of mathematicians is calling for AI labs to do more vetting of discoveries.
They also want them to be presented in a way that a human can understand.
Melanie Matchett Wood is with Harvard.
A lot of the AI mathematical output is doing a very bad job of showing and communicating
its work.
The recommendations came after OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the toughest problems
in mathematics using its AI tools.
Human mathematicians, though, are still trying to untangle the AI's poorly written 166-page
proof to see if it actually found a solution.
Jeff Bronfield, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The family of one of the American citizens shot and killed by federal immigration agents
last January is suing the Trump administration.
The family of Renee Goode alleges federal agents were negligent and violated her civil rights.
Goode was killed in her car as she and her wife were participating in Minneapolis protests
against ICE actions.
Later in January, federal agents also killed Minnesota nurse Alex Priddy.
He was also participating in protests against ICE.
No one has been charged in their killings.
A report on the state of Switzerland's glaciers shows a more than 20 percent loss in ICE volume
over five years.
Imogen Fuchs has more.
The latest figures from Switzerland's National Glacier Monitoring Service show the country's
glaciers lost more than five percent of their volume this year.
An exceptionally hot summer, with repeated heatwaves, took its toll.
The thawing ice eased Europe's drought somewhat.
But when that ice is gone, water for crops and crucial river transport links like the
Rhine and the Danube will be threatened.
Scientists say the link with global warming is clear.
If temperatures continue to rise, Europe's glaciers may not survive this century.
So far, over a thousand Swiss glaciers have already disappeared.
For NPR News, I'm Imogen Fuchs in Bern.
And I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, from Washington.
Stay tuned for the following announcements and messages from our sponsors.
